copy.bottomLine: Productivity is growing faster than in the 2010s: 3.6% at an annual rate last quarter and 2.5% a year since the end of 2023, though not yet beyond normal swings. Through mid-2026, most of the gain came from more capital per hour and people and machines being worked harder; underlying efficiency is too noisy to read. Tech investment is adding about as much to GDP growth as at the dot-com peak, but much of the equipment is imported, and jobs are not shrinking faster where AI use is high. Watch the productivity revision on December 8 and the industry data on December 23.
copy.changed: Latest releases: Q3 Productivity and Costs (BLS, Nov 5) put output per hour up at a 3.6% annual rate. An audit of this page corrected several overstatements: the industry chart's pattern predates AI and no longer counts, and the occupation and investment charts were fixed; the verdict stays Not yet.

caseFor.h: Workers and firms have moved fast.
caseFor.body: About 4 in 10 workers used generative AI for work in the latest surveys, averaging 43% over the last two readings against 36% a year earlier. Business spending on information-processing equipment and software has reached 10.7% of payroll, the highest since the data begin in 1959; the pre-2023 peak was 8.1%.

caseFor.h: Output per hour is pulling away.
caseFor.body: It has grown 2.5% a year since the end of 2023 on both main measures, against 1.6% and 1.4% in 2004–19, and at a 3.6% annual rate in Q3. Chance alone would produce a gap that large only about 10% of the time, down from 22% a quarter ago.

Professional and business services sped up 1.8 points more than retail, leisure and construction, each against its own 2010–19 pace; only 6% of 2010–19 stretches showed a gap that large. Across nine industries, those where more workers use AI have sped up more.

Jobs in computer systems design are down 3.9% since December 2023, while all private jobs rose 1.5%. Only 11% of same-length stretches in 2002–19 were as bad, all of them right after the dot-com bust. Information jobs are down 7.6%.

Workers' share of business income is the lowest on record (the series begins in 1947) and has fallen 1.0% a year since the end of 2023, more than twice its 2004–19 pace. If software and machines are substituting for people, this is where it would show.

caseAgainst.h: No sign of working smarter yet.
caseAgainst.body: Strip out more capital, more skills and harder work, and the SF Fed's figures show underlying efficiency growing about 0.1% a year since the end of 2023, below its 0.6% average in 2004–19. In the 1996–2003 boom it grew about 2.0% a year.

caseAgainst.h: Nothing counted is clear of noise.
caseAgainst.body: No counted test on this page is a clear signal; two are suggestive. Chance alone would put output per hour this far above trend about 10% of the time, and labor's falling share about 35%. Eleven quarters in, output per hour is up 6.9%, against 7.6% at the same point in the 1990s.

caseAgainst.h: The industry and job patterns predate AI.
caseAgainst.body: Office-heavy industries were already pulling ahead in 2019–23, before AI use at work. Young graduates' unemployment was already unusually high next to all workers' by the end of 2022. Across occupations, jobs are not shrinking faster where AI use is higher.

caseAgainst.h: Pay isn't moving the way the AI story predicts.
caseAgainst.body: If AI raised the value of people who direct work, management, business and financial pay should be pulling ahead of office support pay. Instead office pay has grown 4.1% a year since late 2023, against 3.8%, and the ratio is below its 2019 level.

caseAgainst.h: More capital and longer hours explain a lot.
caseAgainst.body: In the SF Fed's Q2 2026 figures, more capital and skills per hour added 1.7 points to 2.3% labor-productivity growth and working harder added another 1.7, while efficiency subtracted 1.1. IT capital is adding only a little more than in 2004–19.

copy.headline: Productivity grew at a 3.6% rate last quarter, but there's no clear sign yet that AI makes work more efficient.

claims.claim: "Evidence is growing that we're turning the corner on productivity. US productivity grew at a 3.6% annual rate this past quarter. That's more than double the 1.5% average from 2007-2019."
claims.check: Q3 was 3.6% and the 2007–19 average 1.5%. But 17% of quarters in 2004–19 were as strong, and the 2.5% pace since the end of 2023 is suggestive, not clear: chance alone would produce it about 10% of the time. Underlying efficiency is flat.

claims.who: Alex Imas, Andrew Koh and Shane Legg, Google DeepMind (Oct 2026)
claims.claim: "Wages and job roles—not headline GDP or industry concentration—remain the earliest signals of change."
claims.check: Computer systems design jobs are down 3.9% since late 2023 against 1.5% growth in all private jobs, which is suggestive. But across occupations, jobs are not shrinking faster where AI use is higher, young graduates' edge has barely narrowed, and management, business and financial pay has slipped relative to office support pay (−0.6%).

claims.claim: "The SF Fed model is showing a slowdown in underlying productivity because it is attributing almost all of the pickup in output/hour to temporary cyclical forces associated with a hot economy."
claims.check: Underlying efficiency has grown about 0.1% a year since the end of 2023, below its 0.6% average in 2004–19, though the estimate is noisy, and working harder added 1.7 points to Q2 2026 growth. Professional and business services have sped up more than hands-on industries, a suggestive signal.
